entry: Northwest Caucasian ethnic group native to Circassia, a region of the North Caucasus. Circassians, also called Cherkess or Adyghe, speak two Circassian languages: western Circassian (Adyghe) and eastern Circassian (Kabardian). Most are Muslim, and [[Sunni Islam]] became dominant in the 17th century. After the 19th-century Russo-Circassian War, most were exiled and scattered across the [[Ottoman Empire]]. Circassian advocates and some historians describe the expulsion as genocide, while Russian narratives frame it as pacification. Today approximately 800,000 Circassians remain in historical Circassia, and 4,500,000 live elsewhere, mostly in [[Turkey]].

Automatic electrical safety device protecting a circuit from overcurrent. Unlike a [[Fuse (electrical)|fuse]], which must be replaced after it operates, a circuit breaker can be reset manually or automatically to resume normal operation. Its basic function is to interrupt current flow to protect equipment and prevent fire, and it is often used as a main switch to disconnect and reconnect power to a whole sub-network. Designs range from devices for low-current circuits and household appliances to switchgear protecting high-voltage circuits that feed an entire city. [[Thomas Edison]] described an early form in an 1879 patent application. A modern miniature circuit breaker was patented by Brown, Boveri & Cie in 1924, and by 1935 breakers at the Boulder Dam project interrupted faults of up to 2,500 MVA in three AC cycles.

Engineering process for designing electrical and electronic circuits, from complex systems down to individual [[Transistor|transistors]]. Traditional design begins with a specification that states what the circuit must do without indicating how, covering signals, power supplies, and physical limits such as size, weight and temperature range. The designer then draws a schematic, calculates component values and runs [[Computer simulation|computer simulation]] to verify the design. A breadboard or other prototype is built and tested against the specification. Changes that conflict with the customer's original specification generally require customer approval. Simple circuits can be designed by one person, but teams using simulation are increasingly common for complex designs. In [[Integrated circuit|integrated circuit]] design automation, the term usually refers to the step that outputs the schematic, between logic design and physical design.

Surgical removal of the [[Foreskin|foreskin]] from the [[Human penis|human penis]]. Performed for religious, cultural, social and medical reasons, it is one of the world's most common and oldest medical procedures; 37–39% of men globally are circumcised. It plays a major role in [[Judaism]] and [[Islam]], and it is considered obligatory in Judaism. Prophylactic use originated in England during the 1850s. It is associated with fewer urinary tract infections and sexually transmitted infections, and it is known to reduce HIV transmission among heterosexual men in high-risk populations by up to 60%. Complication rates rise significantly with age. The [[World Health Organization|World Health Organization]] has recommended it as part of HIV prevention since 2007. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the U.S. CDC conclude that the benefits of newborn circumcision outweigh the risks, while the Royal Australasian College of Physicians and the Canadian Paediatric Society conclude that the benefits do not warrant routine infant circumcision in low-prevalence settings.

Company of performers presenting varied shows of acrobats, [[Clown|clowns]], trained animals and other acts. Newcastle-under-Lyme-born equestrian Philip Astley is credited as the father of the modern circus. In 1768 he began trick horse-riding exhibitions in Ha'penny Hatch, south of the Thames in England, and in 1770 he added acrobats, tightrope walkers, jugglers and a clown, creating the format later named a "circus". The ringmaster-led format of choreographed acts set to music dominated until the 1970s. Since the late 1970s, "new circus" groups have typically avoided animals to focus on human artistry. Many performances still take place in a ring usually 13 m (43 ft) in diameter, a size Astley adopted as the minimum for an acrobatic rider on a cantering [[Horse|horse]].

Amphitheater-like valley formed by glacial erosion. Also called a corrie in Scotland or cwm in Wales. Its concave side is open downhill and enclosed by steep [[Cliff|cliffs]] on three or more sides, and its floor is often overdeepened. A tarn (small lake) often forms on the floor behind a natural dam of [[Moraine|moraine]] or bedrock. A fluvial cirque, or makhtesh, forms in [[Karst|karst]] landscapes, where intermittent river flow cuts through layers of limestone and chalk.

Chronic disease of the [[Liver|liver]] characterized by fibrosis. Scar tissue and regenerative nodules replace functioning liver tissue, increasing resistance to blood flow and causing portal hypertension. The disease typically develops slowly over months or years. Early symptoms include tiredness, weakness, loss of appetite and unexplained weight loss; later symptoms include [[Jaundice|jaundice]], abdominal fluid build-up and easy bruising. Common causes include alcohol-related liver disease, metabolic dysfunction–associated steatohepatitis (MASH), heroin abuse, and chronic hepatitis B and C. Diagnosis relies on blood tests, medical imaging and [[Biopsy|liver biopsy]]. Avoiding alcohol is recommended in all cases, and a liver transplant may be an option once liver failure develops. In 2015 cirrhosis affected about 2.8 million people and caused 1.3 million deaths. [[Hippocrates]] described the condition in the fifth century BCE.

Genus of high-altitude cloud made of ice crystals. Cirrus clouds are delicate, wispy and usually white, forming 6,000 to 20,000 meters above sea level, higher in the tropics and lower in polar regions. They commonly form when warm, dry air rises, and they can form from the tops of [[Thunderstorm|thunderstorms]] and [[Tropical cyclone|tropical cyclones]]. Although they may signal approaching rain or storms, cirrus drop only streaks of ice that evaporate before reaching the ground. Light interacting with the crystals produces [[Halo (optical phenomenon)|halos]] and [[Sun dog|sun dogs]]. Five species are recognized; fibratus is the most common, and uncinus, which is hooked, is called mare's tails. Cirrus-like clouds also form on [[Mars]], the outer planets, and [[Titan (moon)|Titan]], a moon of [[Saturn]].

Genus of perennial and biennial flowering plants in the [[Asteraceae|daisy family]], known as plume thistles. Most species are native to Eurasia and northern Africa, with about 60 from North America. Their seeds bear a feathery pappus that carries them by wind. Many species are considered [[Weed|weeds]]: spear thistle (*Cirsium vulgare*) is a noxious weed in nine U.S. states, where it is called bull thistle. Other species are grown in gardens and wildflower plantings for the nectar that supports bees and butterflies, and the monarch butterfly relies on thistles such as tall thistle (*Cirsium altissimum*) as nectar sources during migration. Some species are used as food in southern Europe, Japan, India and Korea. The name likely derives from the Greek *kirsos*, meaning "swollen vein."

American multinational technology company focused on networking, cybersecurity and AI. Founded in December 1984 by Sandy Lerner and Leonard Bosack, two [[Stanford University|Stanford University]] computer scientists, the company pioneered using a local area network to connect distant computers over a multiprotocol [[Router (computing)|router]] system. It went public in 1990. At the end of the dot-com bubble in 2000 it had a market capitalization of $500 billion, surpassing [[Microsoft]] as the world's most valuable company, before losing 80 percent of its value by 2002.

Waterproof receptacle for holding liquids, usually water. Cisterns are often built to catch and store rainwater, and their interiors are usually lined with hydraulic plaster to prevent leakage. Their waterproof linings distinguish them from [[Well|wells]]. Modern capacities range from a few liters to thousands of cubic meters. Lime-plastered cisterns appear in the floors of [[Neolithic]] village sites in the [[Levant]], and large cisterns served Bronze Age palaces in Israel. Medieval castles in Europe often relied on them where wells could not be dug deep enough. Present-day cisterns are often used for [[Irrigation|irrigation]], and filtration is needed when the water is for drinking.

1941 American drama film directed by and starring [[Orson Welles]]. It was Welles's first feature film, co-written with Herman J. Mankiewicz. The film examines Charles Foster Kane, a composite character based on newspaper publishers [[William Randolph Hearst]] and [[Joseph Pulitzer]]. On release, Hearst banned mention of the film in his newspapers, and it failed to recoup its costs at the box office. It returned to public attention after French critics including André Bazin praised it, and it was re-released in 1956. It is frequently cited as the greatest film ever made: it stood at number one in the British Film Institute's *Sight and Sound* poll for 50 years, and it topped the American Film Institute's *100 Years ... 100 Movies* list in 1998. The film received nine [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nominations and won for Best Writing (Original Screenplay).

Membership in the political community of, and allegiance to, a [[Sovereign state|sovereign state]]. Citizenship is often conflated with nationality in English-speaking countries, though international law does not usually use the term that way. Citizenship generally does not expire and allows a person to work, reside and vote in the state, and it may entitle them to a [[Passport|passport]]. It originated in the rights of urban populations of ancient [[City-state|city-states]] and has since extended to most of a state's people. Recognition may rest on nationality, residence abroad in some countries, or honorary conferment. The civic-republican tradition regards citizenship as active participation in government, while the liberal-individualist conception stresses entitlements necessary for human dignity. Scholars regard its meaning as culture-specific and changing over time. Discriminatory laws, such as disfranchisement and [[Apartheid|apartheid]], have made some citizens second-class.

Interconnected biochemical reactions releasing energy stored in nutrients. Also called the Krebs cycle or TCA cycle, it oxidizes acetyl-CoA to release energy as ATP in organisms that respire. The cycle reduces NAD⁺ to NADH, which feeds oxidative phosphorylation, and each pyruvate molecule yields three NADH, one FADH₂ and one GTP or ATP. In eukaryotic cells it occurs in the [[Mitochondria|mitochondrial]] matrix. Hans Adolf Krebs and William Arthur Johnson identified the cycle in 1937 while at the University of Sheffield, and Krebs received the 1953 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Colorless weak organic acid, C₆H₈O₇, occurring naturally in [[Citrus|citrus]] fruits. It is an intermediate in the [[Citric acid cycle|citric acid cycle]], which occurs in the metabolism of all aerobic organisms. In [[Lemon|lemons]] and [[Lime (fruit)|limes]] it can make up as much as 8% of the dry weight. Industrial production uses fermentation by the mold *Aspergillus niger*, a method discovered in 1917 to be efficient, and remains the major route; global output was in excess of 2,000,000 tons in 2018, more than half of it from China. More than half is used as an acidity regulator in beverages, and it also serves as a flavoring, preservative and chelating agent.

Large, fragrant citrus fruit with a thick, coarse rind. It resembles a [[Lemon|lemon]] but is larger, and it is one of the original citrus fruits from which other citrus types developed through hybridization. Lemons and many [[Lime (fruit)|limes]] were created using citrons. It is used in Asian and Mediterranean cuisine, traditional medicines, perfumes and religious [[Ritual|rituals]]. In Hebrew it is called an *etrog*, and it plays an important role in the harvest holiday of Sukkot.

Genus of flowering trees and shrubs in the family Rutaceae. It includes [[Citron|citrons]], mandarins and pomelos. Many important crops, including [[Orange (fruit)|oranges]], [[Lemon|lemons]], [[Grapefruit]] and [[Lime (fruit)|limes]], were developed through extensive [[Hybrid (biology)|hybridization]]. The genus is native to South Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, Melanesia and Australia, and Indigenous peoples domesticated its species in ancient times. Cultivation spread to the [[Middle East]] and the Mediterranean around 1200 BCE, then from Europe to the Americas. A 2018 DNA study published in *Nature* concluded that the genus evolved in the foothills of the Himalayas, in Assam, western Yunnan and northern Myanmar. Citrus fruits are among the most popular in cultivation, prized for their fragrant aromas and complex flavors.

1931 American romantic comedy-drama film, largely without dialogue, by [[Charlie Chaplin]]. Chaplin wrote, produced, directed and starred in it as his Tramp character, who falls in love with a blind flower girl (Virginia Cherrill) and forms a turbulent friendship with an alcoholic millionaire (Harry Myers). Filming ran from December 27, 1928, to September 1930. Chaplin composed the synchronized score, whose main theme is the song "La Violetera" by Spanish composer José Padilla; Chaplin lost a lawsuit to Padilla for not crediting him. The film was released on March 7, 1931, to positive reviews and worldwide rentals of more than $4 million. In 1949 critic James Agee called its final scene "the greatest single piece of acting ever committed to celluloid." The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the United States National Film Registry in 1991.

Smallest group of buildings surrounded by streets, forming the basic unit of urban fabric. City blocks provide the space for buildings within a city's street pattern, and they may be subdivided into smaller lots, usually privately owned. Cities built on grids have regular rectangular blocks, while many pre-industrial European and Asian cores have irregular ones. In [[Chicago]], a typical block is 330 by 660 feet (100 m × 200 m), so 16 east-west blocks measure one mile. The standard block in Manhattan is about 264 by 900 feet (80 m × 274 m). Blocks in central [[Melbourne]] are also 330 by 660 feet. Exceptions include [[Turin]], founded as a Roman military settlement, and cities heavily damaged in World War II, such as [[Frankfurt]].

Municipality of the Brussels-Capital Region and capital of [[Belgium]] (pop., 2024: 196,828). It is the largest municipality and historical centre of the region, and it is also the capital of the French Community of Belgium, the Flemish Community and the Flemish Region. Its European Quarter hosts a number of principal institutions of the [[European Union|European Union]]. The municipality covers 33.09 sq km and is officially bilingual, in French and Dutch.

2002 Brazilian epic crime film directed by Fernando Meirelles and co-directed by Kátia Lund. Adapted by Bráulio Mantovani from Paulo Lins's 1997 novel, it portrays the rise of [[Organized crime|organized crime]] in the *Cidade de Deus* suburb of [[Rio de Janeiro]] from the late 1960s to the early 1980s. Most of the actors were residents of favelas. It earned four nominations at the 76th Academy Awards, including Best Director and Best Cinematography. In 2015 the Brazilian Film Critics Association ranked it eighth among the 100 greatest Brazilian films. It was followed by the television series *City of Men* and a 2007 film adaptation of that series.

Historic core and [[Central business district|central business district]] of London, England, nicknamed the Square Mile. It covers 2.90 sq km and is the smallest city in the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]] by area. Its population was 8,583 at the 2021 census, and over 500,000 people were employed there as of 2019. Together with Canary Wharf and the West End, it forms London's primary business district. The London Stock Exchange and the Bank of England are based in the City, and the insurance industry has a major presence. The Inns of Court on its western boundary make it a centre for the legal profession.

Sovereign state consisting primarily of a city and its territory. Unlike a country, which typically includes a capital, additional urban centers and the countryside, a city-state encompasses the totality of its sovereign territory. Historical examples include [[Rome]], [[Carthage]], [[Athens]] and [[Sparta]], as well as the Italian city-states of Florence, Venice, Genoa and Milan. Modern city-states are debated, but [[Singapore]], [[Monaco]] and [[Vatican City]] are the candidates most commonly discussed. Singapore is the largest and most populous, and *The Economist* calls it the "world's only fully functioning city-state." Non-sovereign cities with high autonomy, such as [[Hong Kong]] and Macau, are often considered city-states.

Most populous city in the Mexican state of Chihuahua, on the [[Rio Grande|Rio Grande]] south of [[El Paso, Texas|El Paso]], Texas (pop., 2020: 1,512,450). Known until 1888 as El Paso del Norte, it was founded in 1659 by the Franciscan friar García de San Francisco. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ending the [[Mexican–American War|Mexican–American War]] made the Rio Grande the border. Together with El Paso, the city forms the second largest binational metropolitan area on the Mexico–U.S. border, with a combined population of over 3.4 million. More than 300 maquiladoras (assembly plants) operate in and around the city. Violence linked to territorial disputes among drug cartels peaked around 2010, and over 300 homicides were reported in the first three months of 2024 alone.

Study of the rights and obligations of citizens and government. The term derives from the [[Latin|Latin]] *civicus*, meaning "relating to a citizen." Civic education covers the theoretical, political and practical aspects of [[Citizenship|citizenship]], including civil law and the political role of citizens in overseeing government. In ancient [[Sparta|Sparta]], the semi-legendary lawgiver [[Lycurgus|Lycurgus]] made the education of citizens his main priority, training youth in obedience and in judging who was a good citizen. Roman tradition awarded the civic crown, a garland of oak leaves, to those who saved fellow citizens' lives. Simonides compared Spartan education to horse training, since both aimed at obedience to the laws.
